擊木源於非洲，屬古老樂器，近代由古巴及其他南美洲國家發展，成為拉丁與非洲音樂維持: Claves come from Africa and are an old instrument; in modern times they were developed in Cuba and other South American countries into an important percussion instrument for holding the beat steady in Latin and African music. Afro-Cuban son, guaracha and samba often use them to play the fixed 'clave' pattern, and similar instruments are found all over the world. They appear from time to time in classical music from the late Romantic period and more widely in the twentieth century, for example in Varèse's Ionisation (1931) and Reich's Music for Pieces of Wood (1973); the Habanera from Shchedrin's Carmen Suite, after Bizet, is also accompanied by claves. In popular music they are used on recordings such as the Beatles' 'And I Love Her'.
演奏節奏棒時，以一支靜棒、一支動棒配合發聲。非慣用手掌心向上，用拇指與指尖輕托靜: To play claves you need one still stick and one moving stick. Hold the still stick in your non-dominant hand, palm up, resting its middle on the thumb and fingertips; resting it on a fingernail lets the palm form a resonating chamber. Grip the moving stick in the dominant hand the way you hold a drumstick, about a third to a quarter of the way from its end. Strike the centre of the still stick with the end of the moving stick: that gives the loudest, brightest sound. Avoid gripping too tightly at first, or the vibration is damped and the tone goes dull. Traditionally the striking stick is called the male stick and the still stick the female. For a roll, pinch one stick between the thumb and the first two fingers and move it back and forth with alternating pressure, close against the resonating stick, for a continuous sound.

Their range is fairly limited, sitting mainly in the upper middle frequencies, and the interval is not definite. They sound by two wooden sticks striking each other, the wood itself vibrating, so the resonance is plain and dry. Compared with the warm fullness of a xylophone they are more spare; compared with a triangle they lack the metallic sheen. Their sound is strongly rhythmic and incisive, good for underlining the beat and the groove. Because it decays quickly, the result is a short, hard hit — highly expressive, and widely used to carry the rhythm in every kind of music.

The rhythm sticks (claves) are an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.11, originating in Africa and developed in modern times in Cuba and South America. They sound by a pair of short sticks struck together; the sticks are usually about twenty to thirty centimetres long and about two and a half centimetres across, traditionally of rosewood, sandalwood, ebony or African blackwood, and now also of fibreglass or plastic. To play, one stick is cradled in the non-dominant hand to form the resonance while the other is held in the dominant hand and strikes the middle of the first. The sound is short, sharp and crisp, and the instrument is commonly used to keep the rhythm steady in Latin music, African music, large dance orchestras and popular music.
